blindSummary:
Nothing relating to being trans is criminalised in this country, and institutional progress is real: the capital's Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 under heavy (necessary) police protection, and anti-LGBTI hate-crime prosecutors now operate in most sub-national jurisdictions. The counterweights come from a national LGBTI organisation's 2024 report: negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside the capital - especially in the more nationalistic constituent entity, whose leadership is openly hostile - and trans people occupy a "precarious position": no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to the capital and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in the most hostile constituent entity and in rural areas.
blindOutOfScope: Hostility varies between constituent entities; the missing legal gender recognition is resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: Capital-city LGBTI organisation's annual human-rights report on LGBT persons in this country (2024): the position of LGBTI people is unsatisfactory nationwide, with a growing disparity between the country's two constituent entities. In the more nationalist entity there was an organised hooligan attack on Pride marchers in its main city, incitement to violence and discrimination by that entity's highest officials, and organised anti-LGBT groups.

Regional investigative outlet (Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible across this country but described as vague and ineffective in practice - legal texts imply it requires complete medical transition, contradicting self-determination (criticised by a regional parliament). Without documents matching appearance, trans people face difficulties accessing housing and jobs; medical transition becomes a prerequisite for basic rights.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: eight SOGIESC hate-speech cases documented ahead of the capital's Pride; prosecutor offices in the majority of the country's sub-national units now have staff overseeing anti-LGBTI hate crimes; the federal government instructed the justice ministry to draft a same-sex partnership law; the first constitutional-court appeal was filed over non-recognition of a same-sex partnership issued in a neighbouring country; extremists roamed the main city of the nationalist entity chanting death threats before Pride events.

LGBT travel-news archive (2012): a report on gay life in this country - same-sex activity decriminalised in one constituent entity (1996) and the other (1998); the 2009 anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and sexual expression but omitted gender identity; describes a homophobic society across both entities.

Capital-city LGBTI organisation (July 2016): the country's amended anti-discrimination law explicitly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and 'sex characteristics' - the first country in its region to protect intersex people in all spheres; also improves harassment definitions and procedures.

Capital-city LGBTI organisation (July 2016): one of the country's two constituent entities adopted hate-crime provisions covering sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances - all three of the country's top-level administrative units now regulate hate crimes in their criminal codes.
blindLocalsOnly: The missing legal gender recognition framework and restricted healthcare access are resident-facing; the precarious position documented in the 2024 report describes residents' situation.
